title: Rising Stargirls: Benefits of a Creative Arts-Based Approach to Astronomy Education for Middle-School Girls from Underrepresented Groups
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a creative arts-based astronomy program can strengthen science engagement and science identity among middle-school girls, especially girls from groups underrepresented in the sciences. The authors frame middle school as a critical period for sustaining girls’ interest in STEM and argue that arts-integrated, learner-centered science experiences may support persistence and identity development.

The intervention studied is Rising Stargirls, an informal astronomy outreach program that combines astronomy content with free writing, visual art, theater, and other creative activities. The paper analyzes anonymous program-improvement survey data collected before and after workshops run between 2015 and 2023. The workshops were delivered both in person and virtually, primarily for middle-school girls aged 11–14, with many participants identifying as underrepresented minorities. The survey measured self-reported engagement with science and science identity using four Likert-scale items: talking to family and friends about science, enjoyment/excitement about science classes, belief in doing well in science, and seeing oneself as a scientist/science person.

Across the six workshops, the authors report increases in self-reported science engagement and science identity after participation. In both in-person and virtual formats, participants generally reported more frequent science conversations, stronger positive attitudes toward science classes, and greater confidence and identification with science after the workshops. The paper concludes that integrating creativity and the arts into science education may be a promising way to support girls’ interest and identity in science, while also noting that the evidence is based on retrospective self-report surveys from a non-control design.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed retrospective pre/post program evaluation with descriptive nonparametric analyses, but it lacks a control group and random assignment. The study is useful for exploratory evidence, yet credibility is limited by self-report, potential recall bias, and non-equivalent data collection across in-person and virtual formats.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are modest to large on priority outcomes like engagement and science identity, especially in the virtual cohorts where several effect sizes are moderate-to-large. However, the outcomes are attitudinal rather than achievement-based, so the overall impact is promising but indirect for academic attainment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that middle-school girls in Rising Stargirls workshops showed increased science engagement after the intervention. Across all in-person workshops (n=26 pre, n=24 post), talking to family and friends about science increased with Hake’s gain ⟨g⟩=0.2344 and dAw=0.4268; across all virtual workshops (n=66 pre, n=66 post), the same item showed ⟨g⟩=0.4906, cave=0.4958, and dAw=1.0700. The engagement pattern was consistent for science class excitement as well, with virtual workshops showing ⟨g⟩=0.4160 and dAw=0.5900.
finding.measure: Self-reported science engagement: talking to family/friends about science and excitement/liking for science classes on 6-point Likert surveys
finding.study_size: n=126 total workshop participants across 6 workshops; analytic subsamples varied by item (e.g., n=26/24 in-person, n=66/66 virtual)

finding.finding_summary: The program also improved participants’ self-reported science identity, including belief in ability to do well in science and seeing oneself as a science person. For the combined in-person workshops, belief in doing well in science showed essentially no change overall (n=25 pre, n=25 post; ⟨g⟩=-0.0714, dAw=-0.0255), but seeing oneself as a science person increased slightly overall (n=25 pre, n=26 post; ⟨g⟩=0.2582, dAw=0.4463). In the virtual workshops, both items showed moderate-to-large positive gains: belief in doing well in science had ⟨g⟩=0.4500, cave=0.5085, dAw=0.8201, and seeing oneself as a science person had ⟨g⟩=0.3377, cave=0.3593, dAw=0.6235.
finding.measure: Self-reported science self-efficacy and science identity on 6-point Likert surveys
finding.study_size: n=126 total workshop participants across 6 workshops; analytic subsamples varied by item (e.g., n=25/25 in-person, n=66/66 virtual)

finding.finding_summary: Although astronomy was the curricular context, the authors frame the outcomes as broader science attitudes rather than astronomy content mastery. The workshops were associated with stronger agreement that participants liked their science classes and higher confidence/identity as science people, indicating positive development in attitudes toward science learning in general.
finding.measure: Self-reported attitudes toward science classes and science identity
finding.study_size: n=126 total workshop participants across 6 workshops
